standfirst: A savings bank manager who used to be a very effective spy, a daughter who gets taken, and two middle aged friends with one outfit each and the same impossible skill set. It was the biggest broadcast hit of 2026 and it earns the numbers: ten episodes, no romance, no patience for physics. These picks are ranked by how well they deliver the two things that made it work, which are the choreography and the trio.

picks.why: The same lead, the serious version. So Ji Sub walking back into an organisation he left, seven episodes of forty minutes, and violence with actual weight behind it. Better staged and better shot than anything here. Difference: it is noir with no jokes and no friends. The warmth that makes Agent Kim rewatchable is exactly what Mercy for None strips out.

The other 2026 hit about a man with a criminal past applying his skills to a domestic problem. Same mix of comedy, competence and neighbourhood scale stakes, with Ji Sung doing what So Ji Sub does here. Difference: the antagonists are a residents association rather than an intelligence service, so it is smaller, funnier and much less interested in action set pieces.

For the format underneath: a team of specialists, an episodic structure, and people who deserve it getting what is coming on a reliable schedule. Same pleasure in watching unremarkable looking men turn out to be lethal. Difference: it is case of the week pulp with a season long villain who never threatens anyone you like, where Agent Kim runs one continuous plot with a real clock.

Eight episodes of Netflix action where the friendship is the actual subject and the choreography is the reason to watch. Same appetite for hand to hand work you can follow. Difference: it is about two young boxers rather than three tired professionals, and the loan shark plot is thinner than anything in this show. It also has a much worse second season attached.

Revenge with a body cost, eight episodes, no filler. Somebody trained, placed inside an organisation, and visibly damaged by the work, with fight scenes among the best on Netflix Korea. Difference: no comedy and no team. It is bleak, solitary and considerably more violent, and nobody is saved by loyalty.

If the arms trafficking half was what interested you. A former soldier turned police officer, illegal guns circulating through Korea, and a procedural spine holding it together. Difference: it is a lecture as much as a thriller, the pace drops in the middle, and the ending arrives far too quickly to pay off the buildup.

against.title: A Shop for Killers
against.why: The reflex pick for Korean action with a family relationship at the centre. It is a puzzle box told in flashback, deliberately confusing for several hours, and its pleasures are structural. Agent Kim is linear, loud and comic. Anyone arriving from one to the other will find the rhythm completely wrong.

against.title: Vagabond
against.why: Paired for the espionage, and the action really is good. It is also sixteen hours of conspiracy that never resolves, ending on a sequel hook that has never been paid off. This show tells one story in ten hours and closes it. The bloat is the whole difference.

against.title: Good Boy
against.why: Suggested as the other 2025 or later action comedy about a misfit unit. The premise is stronger and the execution is not: sixteen episodes of the same loop, where the team gets beaten, recovers and repeats. Agent Kim wastes nothing. Sending someone from this to Good Boy is sending them from a lean show to a long one.
